title.narrative: Empowering Vulnerable Communities in Syria: Mobile Teams Delivering comprehensive Psychosocial, Educational, and Protection Services in R. Damascus, Aleppo and Latakia

description.narrative: ltpgtIn the heart of communities across Rural Damascus (Babella), Aleppo (Menbij), and Latakia (Qastal Maaf), three dedicated mobile teams from the Community Services and Protection Unit are making a profound impact on the lives of vulnerable individuals. These teams, composed of trained volunteers and case managers, bring essential psychosocial, educational, and protection services directly to those who need them most—wherever they are.ltbrgtAt the core of their work are structured psychosocial programs tailored to different age groups. Children aged 8 to 13 build emotional resilience, while adolescents aged 14 to 17 develop critical life skills. Young adults up to age 45 engage in youth-focused life skills training, and caregivers—often the silent pillars of families—receive support through a specialized program. Even young individuals affected by early marriage are welcomed into this safe and nurturing space. Each program runs for two months, with sessions twice a week, and includes pre- and post-assessments to track improvements in participants’ psychosocial well-being.ltbrgtBeyond these programs, the teams conduct awareness sessions that address pressing issues affecting individuals and families. Adults learn to manage stress and support children through psychological challenges. Sessions on grief, adolescent development, and gender-based violence—including early marriage and the prevention of sexual exploitation—equip communities with knowledge and tools to foster safer, more supportive environments. Protection-focused sessions tackle issues like bullying, child labor, school dropouts, and violence against children, ensuring that no topic is left unspoken.ltbrgtRecognizing the importance of economic empowerment and education, the teams also provide vocational training for individuals over 16 and non-formal education through literacy classes, remedial support, and Homework Cafés. These educational services, delivered by specialized teachers, are tailored to the needs of each community and span up to 200 hours of instruction.ltbrgtInclusion is a guiding principle. Activities for people with disabilities are designed with care—sometimes integrated, sometimes specialized—always respectful of individual needs and capabilities.ltbrgtA cornerstone of the unit’s work is its comprehensive case management system. Cases are identified through various channels: during activities, through self-referral, or via collaboration with other organizations and community members. Once a case is received, a case manager conducts a detailed psychosocial assessment and works with the beneficiary—or their caregiver, in the case of children—to develop a personalized intervention plan. This plan may include referrals to medical, psychosocial, mental health, or livelihood services, all coordinated through a regularly updated network of partners.ltbrgtFollow-up is consistent and compassionate, lasting at least three months and involving regular contact with both the beneficiary and the service providers. When a case concludes—whether due to successful service delivery, relocation, or other reasons—it is carefully documented and, if needed, referred to another organization to ensure continuity of care.ltbrgtThrough this holistic, community-centered approach, the mobile teams of the Community Services and Protection Unit are not just delivering services—they are restoring hope, building resilience, and strengthening the social fabric of communities across Syria.lt/pgt
